part1:
Oil-price news sometimes has a bigger twist in the price movement after an announcement than in the policy announcement itself. This time, the fee plan left the stage, but the price did not leave with it.

On July 13, Trump posted that, for the cost of keeping the Strait of Hormuz safe, the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the strait. A large number suddenly appeared, and it was as if a new main character had entered the news stage.

But the next day, July 14, that main character was quickly replaced. Trump posted that the 20% charge would be replaced by trade and investment deals between the Gulf states and the United States. He explained that the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.
part2:
He also told reporters that no one should charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. He said that he did not like the idea of charging fees itself. The fee plan that appeared the day before had been replaced by another story the next day.

Normally, if the fee story had disappeared, oil prices would also seem likely to settle down. In fact, just after the announcement, Brent crude futures narrowed their gains for a while.

But the price movement did not end there. The price soon returned to a high level close to where it had been before the announcement. At the time the article was published, it was up about 2.6% and above $85 a barrel.
part3:
This return is interesting. The sign had been changed on the political stage, but on the price stage, the price quickly regained its earlier strength. At the same time, attacks between the United States and Iran, a blockade at sea, and worries about tanker safety continued.

What we can see this time is that the words in an announcement may change, while the price does not always move in the same way. Even if the fee plan was replaced, the events continuing at the same time did not simply disappear backstage because of one announcement.
